domain_assessment.domain: Emergency management exercise design and evaluation
domain_assessment.role: Emergency-management exercise planner and full-scale exercise lead
domain_assessment.objective: Design and deliver a HSEEP-compliant levee-failure and flash-flood full-scale exercise, including a Controller-Evaluator handbook and an after-action report that identifies escalation-capability gaps before the seasonal flood window.
domain_assessment.incident_type: Simulated levee failure, dam-break flooding, and flash-flood evacuation requiring multi-agency EOC escalation.

decision_points.summary: The participant set an aggressive project schedule by using a smaller 2019 exercise as the baseline and separately chose the familiar legacy scenario template over a proposed modular format.
evidence_before: The 2019 exercise took about six weeks.
The earlier project had two staff members and reused an existing scenario shell.
The current project had one planner, a larger footprint, a new hydrology module, updated dam-break modeling, and coordination with three agencies.
The current deadline was fixed at ten weeks.
evidence_after: Four weeks into the project, the participant was still building the custom module and awaiting three-agency sign-off.
A status check showed a two-week schedule slip.
The participant later recognized that separately estimating agency-sign-off hours would likely have led to more schedule padding.
goals_constraints: Produce a full exercise day, usable Controller-Evaluator handbook, and useful AAR.
Work solo despite a larger scope.
Coordinate with the regional EOC, school district, police, and fire agencies.
alternatives: Build a formal contingency buffer and separately estimate new-module and multi-agency coordination work.
Compress the new work into the prior project window.
Use the newly proposed modular design format.
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant relied heavily on the prior project's duration and on familiarity with the legacy template, while making only limited adjustment for the changed staffing and scope.
decision_points.time_pressure: Moderate at kickoff; high after the status check revealed a two-week slip.
decision_points.uncertainty: The participant had not yet decomposed the time required for three-agency approval or custom hydrology development, and had no comparative outcome evidence for the modular versus legacy format.

decision_points.summary: The participant calibrated scenario severity downward from updated catastrophic dam-failure modeling toward a familiar local flood level, then did not apply equivalent scrutiny to that choice while criticizing a peer's insufficiently demanding scenario.
evidence_before: Updated Army Corps modeling indicated a higher catastrophic dam-failure risk than previously used.
The advisory committee emphasized that flooding of that severity had not occurred locally for more than forty years.
A peer planner's mild scenario had been criticized because it did not stress escalation procedures.
evidence_after: The participant scaled peak severity down toward the familiar flood level.
The participant acknowledged that the forty-year historical-absence point shaped the decision.
The participant acknowledged not applying the same scrutiny to the concurrent severity decision that was applied to the peer's design.
goals_constraints: Keep the scenario credible and plausible to community stakeholders.
Reconcile updated technical hazard information with stakeholder expectations.
Make a severity decision during an already slipping schedule.
alternatives: Use the catastrophic severity indicated by updated modeling.
Use a more familiar, historically experienced flood severity.
Create a graduated or tiered scenario that preserves catastrophic escalation testing while retaining locally recognizable early injects.
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant gave substantial weight to historical local non-occurrence and perceived plausibility, despite the newer risk model, and did not independently re-evaluate the resulting severity decision when exposed to an analogous peer failure.
decision_points.time_pressure: High because the schedule had slipped and remaining production choices were becoming constrained.
decision_points.uncertainty: It remains uncertain whether the milder scenario actually reduced escalation testing or whether exercise-day conditions caused the apparent performance limitations.

decision_points.summary: With time to fully build only one inject category, the participant allocated most remaining production effort to visual photo and video injects rather than operationally specific data packages.
evidence_before: Photo and video clips of overtopping were dramatic but slow to produce.
Data packages containing stream-gauge readouts and GIS flow-rate shapefiles were less visually interesting but more specific for EOC modeling decisions.
Past surveys indicated that participants remembered visual materials vividly.
evidence_after: Most remaining time went to photo and video injects.
The participant later stated that the decision emphasized impact and recall more than whether decision-makers would have the required flow-rate specifics when needed.
goals_constraints: Produce usable training injects before the fixed deadline.
Select one category that could be fully developed.
Support exercise participation and operational EOC decision-making.
alternatives: Prioritize photo and video overtopping injects.
Prioritize stream-gauge and GIS flow-rate data packages.
Split limited production effort across both formats, accepting reduced completeness.
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant treated memorability and visual impact as the primary criterion, rather than explicitly weighting the formats against the operational information requirements of the decisions being evaluated.
decision_points.time_pressure: Very high; production capacity permitted full development of only one inject category.
decision_points.uncertainty: The interview does not establish whether visual recall translated into better operational performance or whether data packages would have materially improved the evaluated decisions.

decision_points.summary: The participant kept the Controller-Evaluator handbook concise and omitted a glossary despite prior informal feedback that evaluators outside core emergency management needed clearer explanations of specialist terminology.
evidence_before: The participant had fifteen years of experience using the same shorthand and scoring conventions.
Past AAR feedback had informally requested clearer explanations for evaluators outside core emergency management.
The handbook had to be completed under severe time pressure.
evidence_after: The participant omitted a glossary and retained standard shorthand.
The participant stated that the terminology felt standard to them.
The participant later recognized that a planner without the same fifteen years of habits might not assume the terms were obvious.
The participant appropriately remained uncertain whether scoring inconsistencies were caused by shorthand or by other factors.
goals_constraints: Complete a usable Controller-Evaluator handbook before the exercise deadline.
Support evaluators with mixed levels of emergency-management experience.
alternatives: Retain the concise handbook without a glossary.
Add a brief glossary or plain-language explanation of scoring conventions.
Use an abbreviated glossary limited to terms previously identified as unclear.
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant treated personally familiar specialist terminology as sufficiently self-evident despite audience-specific feedback indicating lower familiarity among some evaluators.
decision_points.time_pressure: Very high; the handbook was completed close to the fixed deadline.
decision_points.uncertainty: The causal contribution of shorthand to scoring inconsistencies is explicitly unresolved and may be confounded by multiple exercise-day factors.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “I looked at the 2019 project — six weeks, two staff, reused shell — and treated that as roughly the baseline. I adjusted a little for the new module, but not by much.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Decision-point-1 timeline reconstruction and follow-up probe concerning confidence in the compressed schedule.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant used the duration of a materially smaller, better staffed, and partly reused prior project as the practical baseline for the current estimate, while insufficiently incorporating known scope expansion, reduced staffing, custom development, and multi-agency approval work. The later admission that agency sign-off was not separately estimated supports a deficient duration-estimation process rather than merely an unfavorable result.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: A fixed ten-week calendar deadline may have constrained the stated delivery commitment, and experienced planners can sometimes legitimately use analogical estimates. However, the participant expressly reports limited adjustment despite known disanalogies and omission of a separately identifiable workload component.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: None required. A formal estimate record would further corroborate the episode but is not necessary for a supported occurrence.

revision.location: Decision point 1, participant responses beginning “Right, so going in...” and “Honestly, mostly that I'd done a version of this before...”
revision.current_defect: No material defect; the interview supplies the reference-class facts, insufficient adjustment, omitted contingency, and subsequent schedule evidence.
preserve: The distinction between the 2019 project and the current project.
The participant's limited adjustment rather than an explicit claim of irrationality.
The separate format-preference episode at the same decision point.
avoid_creating: An explicit textbook statement that the participant was overoptimistic.
A stronger claim that the deadline slip proves the bias.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “But I went with the legacy template again — third cycle running it. It's the one I know, I can build it fast, and honestly it's just more comfortable to work in.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Decision-point-1 scenario-format exchange immediately after the schedule-estimation discussion.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant selected the repeatedly used legacy format partly because repeated exposure had produced familiarity and comfort, while acknowledging no formal comparative evidence about whether the alternative modular format produced better or worse training outcomes. This is a selection episode distinct from the schedule estimate: it concerns format preference rather than duration prediction.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The familiar template may genuinely have reduced production cost under a severe deadline, making the choice partly justified as risk management or operational efficiency. The bias signal remains supported because the participant also identifies comfort and repeated use as reasons and did not compare the alternatives' training performance.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: No additional evidence is required, although a brief indication that the modular format was operationally feasible within the same design environment would make the preference-versus-efficiency distinction still cleaner.

revision.location: Decision point 1, participant answer beginning “Yeah, there was a newer modular design format...” and the subsequent question about comparative training outcomes.
revision.current_defect: No material defect; the episode establishes repeated exposure, familiarity, an alternative, and absent comparative evidence.
preserve: The participant's acknowledgement that the legacy template was more comfortable.
The lack of formal comparative training-outcome data.
avoid_creating: A claim that the modular format was objectively superior.
An additional status-quo or loss-aversion episode based on the same format choice.
A merger with the timeline-estimation rationale.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “I ended up scaling the peak severity down toward the more familiar flood level. The forty-year point came up a lot in that conversation, and it did shape my thinking — if nobody's seen anything like the catastrophic case, it felt like we were designing for something abstract rather than something the EOC would actually face.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Decision-point-2 severity-calibration exchange following the contrast between updated Corps modeling and forty years without a similarly severe local event.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant discounted or downweighted updated catastrophic-risk modeling because the event was not within recent local experience and therefore felt implausible or abstract. The reasoning is about normalizing expected conditions from historical familiarity, not simply about valid community-facing scenario design.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: A full-scale exercise may legitimately need a scenario that stakeholders regard as credible and executable. That explanation does not fully account for the participant's explicit move from the absence of recent experience to reduced weight on the current hazard model, particularly where the objective was to validate escalation procedures.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: None required. The interview already identifies the conflicting evidence source, the historical framing, and the way the participant weighted that framing.

revision.location: Decision point 2, participant response beginning “I ended up scaling the peak severity down...”
revision.current_defect: No material defect; the text gives a specific evidence-weighting mechanism rather than relying on the eventual exercise result.
preserve: The updated Corps modeling as the competing risk evidence.
The advisory committee's forty-year historical-absence framing.
The distinct peer-review episode that follows.
avoid_creating: A claim that a catastrophic scenario was necessarily the correct operational choice.
A second normality-bias occurrence through repeated references to local plausibility.
A merger with the self-versus-other scrutiny episode.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “In that discussion I was pretty clear it looked like a planning gap on their end. I wasn't especially worried about the same thing happening with my build, even though I was mid-decision on my own severity call at that exact time.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Decision-point-2 peer AAR review exchange and the immediately following self-scrutiny probe.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant evaluated a peer's mild scenario as reflecting a planning failure but did not subject the participant's concurrent, analogous severity-reduction decision to equivalent scrutiny. The later admission—“Not in that moment”—makes the asymmetry in self-versus-other evaluation directly observable.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The peer exercise may have differed materially in design facts, severity evidence, or operational objectives. The interview, however, presents the peer problem specifically as an unrealistically mild scenario that failed to stress escalation procedures and situates the participant's analogous calibration decision at the same time.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: None required. The current probe explicitly tests whether equivalent scrutiny was applied and receives a direct negative answer.

revision.location: Decision point 2, participant response about the peer AAR and answer to “Did you apply the same scrutiny...?”
revision.current_defect: No material defect; the self-other comparison is explicit and analytically distinct from the severity-calibration mechanism.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain both the peer-review account and the direct self-scrutiny probe.
preserve: The temporal overlap between the peer review and the participant's own severity decision.
The participant's acknowledgement of unequal scrutiny.
avoid_creating: A generic attribution-error claim unsupported by dispositional language.
A hindsight-based criticism of the participant's decision outcome.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “I put most of the remaining time into the photo and video injects. Past surveys showed people remember those vividly — I figured that made them the more effective training tool.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Decision-point-3 inject-allocation response and follow-up concerning support for actual evaluator decisions.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant translated vivid recall of visual materials into a preference for visual injects as training tools, while giving insufficient weight to the data packages' direct relevance to stream-flow and EOC modeling decisions. The relevant reasoning error is not that images are memorable—they often are—but that memorability was used as a dominant proxy for operational training value without an evidentiary bridge.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Visual injects can legitimately promote engagement, shared situational awareness, and retention, especially in an exercise setting. The bias classification is supported because the participant explicitly states that recall drove the effectiveness inference and concedes that decision-specific information availability was underweighted.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: None required for support. A concise statement that evaluators specifically needed flow-rate inputs at a defined decision stage would further sharpen the operational-relevance contrast.

revision.location: Decision point 3, participant responses beginning “I put most of the remaining time...” and “Less than I probably should have...”
revision.current_defect: No material defect; the episode includes a clear allocation decision, a recall-based rationale, a data-rich alternative, and an acknowledged operational-relevance omission.
preserve: The genuine past-survey finding about vivid recall.
The distinction between memorability and operational decision support.
avoid_creating: A claim that visual learning is inherently ineffective.
A second allocation decision involving the same visual materials.
A retrospective assertion that the visual injects caused poor exercise performance.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “There'd been informal feedback in past AARs asking for clearer explanations for evaluators outside core EM, yeah. But the terms felt pretty standard to me, so I didn't prioritize adding that layer given how little time was left.”
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant's long-term familiarity with emergency-management shorthand led them to treat terms as self-evident for a mixed-experience evaluator audience, despite audience-specific feedback that clearer explanations were needed. This is a calibration failure about others' knowledge state, not merely an ordinary omission under deadline pressure.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The glossary may have been reasonably deprioritized because of the acute deadline, and the feedback was informal rather than a definitive usability study. However, the participant's stated reason includes the terms feeling standard to them despite known lower familiarity among some evaluators, which directly supports the mechanism.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: None required. The text already establishes specialist expertise, the mixed-background audience, prior feedback, and the participant's self-referential assessment of term obviousness.

revision.location: Decision point 4, participant answers concerning fifteen years of shorthand use and prior feedback about clearer explanations.
revision.current_defect: No material defect; the episode is independently identifiable and does not depend on uncertain outcome attribution.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the handbook episode as written.
preserve: The participant's fifteen years of experience.
The prior feedback from evaluators outside core emergency management.
The time-pressure constraint and later causal uncertainty.
avoid_creating: A claim that all handbook scoring inconsistencies were caused by jargon.
A generalized expert-overconfidence episode beyond the terminology-calibration decision.
An explicit use of the phrase “curse of knowledge” in participant dialogue.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “I looked at the 2019 project ... and treated that as roughly the baseline. I adjusted a little for the new module, but not by much.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: The prior six-week project duration served as an initial numerical reference point that was insufficiently adjusted for the current project's dissimilarities.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Using a comparable prior project as an initial estimate is normal professional practice. The evidence is better classified under the requested Planning Fallacy because the consequential error concerns duration estimation under insufficient adjustment, not a separately observable anchor-and-adjust episode.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “If nobody's seen anything like the catastrophic case, it felt like we were designing for something abstract rather than something the EOC would actually face.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: Absence of personally or locally memorable severe flooding may have reduced the subjective salience of the catastrophic scenario.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The participant refers to local historical occurrence and stakeholder plausibility, not explicitly to ease of recalling vivid examples. The episode is more directly and sufficiently captured as Normality Bias; treating it as a separate availability occurrence would double count the same evidence trace.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “Whether the milder scenario actually undercut the escalation testing, or whether it was just a rough exercise day for other reasons — I genuinely don't know.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: No supported outcome-bias mechanism is present; the participant expressly avoids judging decision quality solely by the exercise result.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The participant demonstrates appropriate causal restraint and acknowledges alternative explanations.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “The terms felt pretty standard to me.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: The participant's expertise may have increased confidence that specialist terminology was understandable.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The evidence concerns failure to model the audience's knowledge state, which is more precisely Curse of Knowledge. It does not independently establish excessive confidence in the participant's own competence or correctness.

nonbias_cues.cue: The project slipped two weeks and became a scramble.
nonbias_cues.location: Chronological incident account following the first four weeks of work.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: A schedule slip is an outcome, not evidence of a cognitive mechanism. It becomes relevant only because the participant later describes the estimation process and omitted coordination breakdown.

nonbias_cues.cue: The participant was solo, had a larger scope, needed custom hydrology work, and faced three-agency sign-off.
nonbias_cues.location: Initial incident account and chronology reconstruction.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: These are real workload and organizational constraints. They explain why the project was difficult but do not themselves demonstrate biased reasoning.

nonbias_cues.cue: The deadline was fixed by the flood-risk calendar.
nonbias_cues.location: Initial project description and decision-point chronology.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Time pressure can alter prioritization and make compromises rational; it is not itself evidence of any listed bias.

nonbias_cues.cue: The advisory committee wanted a scenario the community would find plausible.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Stakeholder acceptability can be a legitimate exercise-design objective. The bias evidence comes specifically from downweighting updated risk modeling because severe local events had not been experienced recently.

nonbias_cues.cue: Past surveys showed that participants remembered visual injects vividly.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: The reported recall difference may be true. The relevant bias is the unvalidated inference that recall should dominate selection despite the data package's decision-specific utility.

nonbias_cues.cue: The participant had fifteen years of experience using the same shorthand.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Experience is not a bias. It supports a Curse-of-Knowledge interpretation only when paired with evidence that the participant assumed others shared that knowledge despite contrary audience feedback.

nonbias_cues.cue: The participant is uncertain whether scenario severity or handbook shorthand caused observed exercise weaknesses.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: This is appropriate causal uncertainty, not hindsight, rationalization, or evasion. It avoids unsupported single-cause attribution.

causal_claims.claim: The compressed timeline estimate contributed to the project schedule slip.
causal_claims.support: The participant used a smaller prior project as a baseline, made limited adjustments for known dissimilarities, omitted a contingency buffer, and later found that unseparated multi-agency sign-off work had contributed to the slip.
causal_claims.assessment: Moderately supported as a process-level causal contribution, not established as the sole cause.

causal_claims.claim: Prioritizing photo and video injects reduced availability of data needed for operational EOC modeling decisions.
causal_claims.support: The participant states that most remaining production time was allocated to visuals and later concedes that the flow-rate specifics might not have been available when needed.
causal_claims.assessment: Strongly supported as a resource-allocation consequence; the downstream effect on exercise performance remains unmeasured.

causal_claims.claim: The milder scenario may have undercut escalation testing.
causal_claims.support: A peer's mild scenario reportedly failed to stress escalation procedures, and the participant's own scenario was scaled downward.
causal_claims.assessment: Appropriately unresolved. The participant explicitly identifies alternative explanations and does not claim causation from the available evidence.

causal_claims.claim: Handbook shorthand may have caused scoring inconsistencies.
causal_claims.support: Prior feedback requested clearer terminology for non-core emergency-management evaluators, but the participant states that scoring inconsistencies could have arisen from many causes.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Treating the schedule slip as proof that the initial estimate was biased.
correlation_causation_risks.mitigation_present: The interview identifies multiple operational contributors—custom development, agency approvals, and fixed timing—rather than relying on the outcome alone.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Treating vivid recall of visual injects as proof of superior operational training.
correlation_causation_risks.mitigation_present: The interviewer directly probes the difference between memorability and support for operational decisions, and the participant acknowledges the distinction.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Treating a rough exercise day as proof that reduced severity or handbook shorthand caused deficiencies.
correlation_causation_risks.mitigation_present: The closing response explicitly preserves alternative explanations and causal uncertainty.

causal_audit.explanation: The interview contains retrospective hypotheticals—such as what the participant might have done with two additional weeks and what a different planner might have questioned—but it does not present a paired or controlled counterfactual design with a designated changed causal variable. Within the observed narrative, causal claims are generally restrained: process mechanisms are evidenced, while uncertain downstream performance effects are explicitly not overattributed.

global_revision_constraints: Do not count the same schedule-estimation episode again as a separate Anchoring occurrence unless the manifest is intentionally expanded and a distinct evidence trace is added.
Do not count the same severity-calibration episode again as a separate Availability Heuristic occurrence; its current evidence is most defensibly allocated to Normality Bias.
Preserve the participant's explicit uncertainty about whether scenario severity and handbook shorthand caused downstream exercise deficiencies.
Do not strengthen participant language by naming biases or by making outcomes appear determinative; the existing evidence is sufficiently subtle and mechanism-specific.
Maintain the separation between decision point 1's duration estimation and format selection, and decision point 2's severity calibration and self-versus-other scrutiny.
